question: How do I hide the Find Friends panel in the Spotify app on my Mac?
reference_answer: Click View and uncheck Right Sidebar.

answer.answer: In the Spotify Mac app (as of late 2017), Spotify support said you can hide the Find Friends section by clicking View and unchecking Right Sidebar. That hides the right sidebar, which includes the Find Friends panel. The interface may have changed since then.

verification.feedback: All claims are supported by the SpotifyCares reply; no changes needed.

grade.rationale: The answer matches SpotifyCares’ instruction to click View and uncheck Right Sidebar, and the extra note that this hides the right sidebar containing Find Friends is a fair paraphrase of that reply.

question: UPS says my package will arrive by 'end of day'. What time does that mean?
reference_answer: UPSHelp said end of day is 7 PM (delivery times run 9am to 7pm), though drivers can be out later in some areas.

answer.answer:
UPS agents in 2017 did not give one fixed clock time for “end of day,” and answers differed.

Most often they said end of day is typically around 7:00 PM, but delivery can be later depending on the driver’s route, volume, or load, and drivers stay out until the packages on the truck are delivered ([#346702], [#213025], [#404995], [#271885]).

Other agents gave later cutoffs: one said drivers can be out as late as 10 PM if not later ([#171101]); another said they try to finish before midnight, but midnight is the end of the day ([#397555]).

This is from October–November 2017 and may have changed since.

verification.feedback: No change needed. Each delivery-time claim is a fair paraphrase of a UPS agent in the cited 2017 threads, and the October–November 2017 note needs no citation.

grade.rationale: Every claim is supported by the cited UPSHelp replies: most agents said end of day is typically around 7 PM but deliveries can run later, and two agents gave later cutoffs of 10 PM or midnight. That conveys the reference’s key point that end of day is about 7 PM with later deliveries possible.

question: I forgot to cancel my Amazon Prime free trial and got charged. Can I get that money back?
reference_answer: AmazonHelp said that if you haven't used any Prime benefits since the charge you get a full refund; otherwise the refund is pro-rated. They linked the help page for cancelling the membership.

answer.answer:
Yes, according to Amazon support in 2017, you can cancel after a forgotten Prime free-trial charge and may get money back. What agents said differed:

- In [#541778], an agent said you can expect a full refund as long as none of the benefits were used after switching to the paid membership.
- In [#249833], an agent said if you haven’t used the benefits since being charged, you’ll receive a full refund; otherwise it will be pro-rated.
- In [#359060], an agent said if no benefits have been used, you can cancel for a full refund.
- In [#155139], an agent said a refund will be issued for the unused benefits (they did not spell out a full-vs-pro-rated rule).
- In [#43937], an agent only said it was not too late to cancel and possibly get a refund.
- In [#426971], an agent said you can end Prime and get any available refund.

Agents pointed people to cancel in Your Account or via a Help page rather than processing the refund in the tweet. This is from October–November 2017 and may have changed since.

verification.feedback: No fix needed. Each refund rule is a fair paraphrase of the cited AmazonHelp agent, and the 2017 date note needs no support.

grade.rationale: Every refund claim matches an AmazonHelp agent in the cited tweets, including the full-refund-if-unused and otherwise-pro-rated rule that is the reference's main point. Extra citations add supported detail and do not contradict it.

question: I bought a product at Sainsbury's that turned out to be bad. How do I get a refund?
reference_answer: Sainsbury's either asks you to take it back to the store with your receipt for an exchange or refund, or asks which store it was from (and sometimes for a barcode photo) and then for your Nectar card number by DM so they can add the refund, sometimes with extra, as points.

answer.answer:
Sainsbury’s Twitter agents in late 2017 did not state one fixed refund rule. What they told customers varied by case:

- A soggy berry fruit pot: they asked for the barcode and which store, then for the customer’s full name and Nectar card number by DM so they could feed it back and add a refund [#252289].
- Sausages with already-split packaging: they asked for a photo of the barcode and which store, then only the Nectar card number by DM, and said they would add a refund and feed it back [#549171].
- An out-of-date item (the product itself was not identified): the customer had no receipt and did not plan to return to the store. The agent only asked for full name and Nectar card number by DM and offered to add a refund. They did not ask for a barcode or say they would log the issue [#298154].
- A sound bar with awful sound, receipt still held: return to the store with the receipt for a refund [#160720].
- A charger that would not charge a phone, no receipt, paid by card: take the card and the product back to the store so they could get a duplicate receipt, and tell them the product is faulty [#721776].
- General advice, not tied to a particular product: if there is no receipt but the purchase was on a bank card, a bank statement showing the product price or higher can be used as proof of purchase, and the store can track the transaction even if other items were bought at the same time [#748771].
- A portable record player with awful quality, bought the day before, receipt held: take it back to the store for a refund or exchange as long as it is in a resellable condition [#629001].

In the first three cases, agents used the Nectar number (and sometimes the name) to add the refund; they did not call the Nectar number proof of purchase. This is from October–November 2017 and may have changed.

unsupported_claims: A soggy berry fruit pot (only the customer said the fruit was soggy; the agent did not).
Sausages with already-split packaging (only the customer described the packaging).
An out-of-date item, and that the customer had no receipt and did not plan to return (customer statements only; the agent did not confirm them or name the product).
A sound bar with awful sound, receipt still held (the agent did not confirm sound quality or that the receipt was held).
A charger that would not charge a phone, no receipt, paid by card (customer statements; the agent did not confirm no receipt).
A portable record player with awful quality, bought the day before, receipt held (the agent did not state quality, purchase date, or receipt).
Agents used the Nectar number (and sometimes the name) to add the refund (they only asked for those details and said they would add a refund).
verification.feedback: Keep only what the agents said. Mark product condition, receipts, payment method, and purchase timing as the customer’s report, or drop them. Say the agents asked for the Nectar number (and sometimes the name) and offered to add a refund; do not say they used that number to add one.

grade.rationale: Every case in the system answer is fairly supported by the cited Sainsbury’s agents, including store returns with a receipt, Nectar-card DMs to add a refund, and card/bank-statement proof. It conveys the reference’s main point that refund handling varied between an in-store return and a remote Nectar refund.
